newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany vows to have another crack at tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: Germany vows to have another crack at tax reforms.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government vowed on Thursday to have another crack at pushing through sweeping tax reform legislation, just hours after parliament's mediation committee had thrown out the plans.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he had agreed with Kohl that the ruling coalition should ask parliament to send the 30 billion mark ($16.3 billion) tax-cutting package back to the committee for a second time.

The committee, which is called in when the two houses of parliament cannot agree on legislation, failed to reach a compromise on the government's plans after marathon talks which lasted into the early hours of Thursday morning.
Waigel turned the heat on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who blocked the bill in the upper house and used their majority on the mediation committee to reject a compromise.
"We'll keep the big tax reform on the agenda," he told a news conference in Bonn, insisting the government still wanted to bring in as much of the reform as possible.
"If this doesn't happen, then the SPD alone must bear the responsibility." he said. "The SPD is moving at a snail's pace when it comes to tax reform."

The SPD said it saw little chance of a compromise on the tax plan, intended to stimulate foreign investment and make Germany more competitive within Europe's planned economic and monetary union, unless the government made major concessions.
"I fear this mediation process will end the same way the last one ended last night," SPD chief whip Peter Struck said. "We're prepared to talk but I'm very sceptical."
The only thing the late-night talks managed to produce was an agreement to scrap a capital trading tax on companies and compensate local governments for lost revenues.

The opposition majority in the mediation committee also backed SPD proposals to cut the cost of employing workers by slashing occupational insurance charges from this October and raising indirect taxation to pay for the changes.

The committee's decision sets in train a complicated parliamentary procedure. Deputies in the lower house will break from their holidays to hold a special session on Tuesday to vote on the mediation committee's decisions.
Barring any major surprises, parliament will approve the abolition of the capital trading tax and Kohl will use his majority to reject the committee's other proposals.

The package then goes back to the upper house for its next sitting in September, where the SPD can reject it a second time. Only then can the lower house formally call in the mediation committee to have another crack at the plans.
